genres.name: Bhangra
genres.note: Bhangra originated as a harvest folk dance and music tradition of the Punjab (both Indian and Pakistani sides), associated with the Vaisakhi festival. After Partition (1947) the style spread with Punjabi migrants to UK cities where it blended with reggae, hip-hop and dancehall ('bhangra beat') in the 1980s–90s. The Rough Guide (2000) notes that by this period 'female artists compete for record sales', confirming the genre's commercial vitality. Today bhangra is an internationally recognized dance-music genre, prominent in Bollywood, British Asian pop, and diaspora communities.

sources.citation: Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

associated_areas.note: Pakistan’s UNESCO periodic report identifies Bhangra among Punjab folk music practices. The report date is a documentation anchor, not an origin date. Approximate prominence end; not an extinction claim. No later activity boundary is stated; a four-decade prominence/documentation window is used as the editorial fallback.

genres.name: Kalbelia songs
genres.note: Kalbelia is a folk song and dance tradition of the Kalbelia (snake charmer) community of Rajasthan. Inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2010, the style is characterized by sinuous, snake-like dance movements and songs evoking the community's itinerant lifestyle, accompanied by the been (double-pipe instrument) and dholak drums. Gulabo Sapera is the most internationally recognized Kalbelia dancer, and the tradition continues to be performed at festivals across Rajasthan.

sources.citation: Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

genres.name: Manipuri Sankirtana
genres.note: Sankirtana is a ritual singing, drumming and dancing tradition of Manipur, performed at life-cycle events, festivals, and religious occasions to pay homage to the god Vishnu. Inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2013, it involves elaborate costumes, large double-headed pung drums, and cymbals. The tradition is maintained by specialist sangha communities in Manipur and remains an integral part of Meitei cultural identity.

sources.citation: Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

genres.name: Buddhist chanting of Ladakh
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Ladakhi Buddhist ritual chanting encompasses the ceremonial music of Tibetan Buddhist monasteries in the Ladakh region of Jammu & Kashmir. Performed at annual monastic festivals such as Hemis, Thiksey and Lamayuru, the tradition uses long telescoping dungchen horns, gyaling shawms, gyaling horns, large frame drums, and multi-octave throat-singing to accompany masked Cham dances and recitation of scriptures. The tradition is actively maintained by monastic institutions and draws both pilgrims and international visitors.

sources.citation: Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

genres.name: Garba of Gujarat
genres.note: Garba is a circular dance-and-song tradition of Gujarat, performed especially during the nine-night Navratri festival in honour of the goddess Amba. Inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2023, Garba remains one of the most widely participated folk art forms in India. The tradition combines devotional song (garba songs), clapping patterns, and stick-dance (dandiya raas), and has expanded into large outdoor festival events across Gujarat and in diaspora communities worldwide.

sources.citation: Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

genres.name: Bhatiyali
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Bhatiyali is a genre of river boat songs from Bangladesh, sung by boatmen (majhi) drifting downstream on the great river systems of the Bengal delta — the Padma, Meghna, and Brahmaputra. The melodies reflect the meditative state of river travel, with slow, undulating, microtonal passages evoking the movement of water. Associated with Sufi mysticism and Baul philosophy, bhatiyali uses simple melodic structures that allow for extensive improvisation. The tradition is maintained by village musicians and folk performers across the Sylhet, Mymensingh and Dhaka regions.

sources.citation: Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

genres.note: Bhawaiya (also bhaoyaiya) is a traditional folk song genre of the Rangpur and Cooch Behar districts of northern Bengal (now straddling Bangladesh and West Bengal, India). The songs typically lament the absence of a husband or lover (sung from a woman's perspective) and are associated with the bullock-cart drivers (garial) of the region. The dotara lute is the primary accompanying instrument. The form is still practiced by folk musicians in North Bengal and is performed at rural fairs and cultural programs.

genres.note: Rabindra Sangeet (Tagore songs) is a body of approximately 2,232 songs composed by Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941), encompassing devotional, romantic, seasonal, and patriotic themes. Two of Bangladesh's national songs are Tagore compositions. The form is rigorously maintained through the Rabindra Sangeet performance tradition, with leading contemporary artists including Rezwana Chowdhury Banya who performs and teaches extensively in Dhaka. Tagore's birthday (Pahela Boishakh) and death anniversary (Baishey Shravan) are major annual occasions for performances across Bangladesh and West Bengal.

genres.note: Qawwali is the devotional music of Sufi Islam, developed in South Asia from the 13th century through the teachings of the poet-saint Amir Khusrau. It is performed in praise of Allah, the Prophet, and Sufi saints at shrines (dargahs) across Pakistan and India, led by a hereditary lead singer (qawwal) with a supporting chorus, harmonium, tabla and dholak. The Rough Guide (2000) states 'the traditional strains of qawwali continue to flourish' even after the death of its greatest exponent, Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan (1997), with the Rizwan-Muazzam Qawwali Group performing at international festivals such as WOMAD.

image.depicts: Khattak is a swift martial sword-dance of the Khattak tribe of Pashtuns in Pakistan and Afghanistan. It is one of the Pashtun folk dances known as Atanr, not the classical Indian style of dance known as Kathak. Katthak is danced to fast music featuring the piper clarion and drums beaten with sticks. Up to 40 men dance together wielding swords or handkerchiefs, performing acrobatic feats. The fast tempo of Khattak distinguishes it from other Atanr which start slow and pick up speed as the dance progresses. Khattak dancers also lack Sanrry, the distinctive hairstyle.

genres.name: Kandyan drumming
genres.note: Kandyan drumming (Udarata drumming) is the ceremonial percussion tradition of the central highlands of Sri Lanka, centered on the historic kingdom of Kandy. The principal drum is the double-headed geta bera, played with two different techniques on each head. Performances accompany the annual Esala Perahera procession — one of Asia's largest Buddhist pageants — and temple festivals throughout the Kandyan region. Hereditary drummers (berava caste) maintain the tradition, which the Rough Guide (2000) notes is inseparable from Sri Lanka's Buddhist ritual life.

sources.citation: Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

image.depicts: Kandyan Dance is today considered the national dance of Sri Lanka. The male dancers wear a wide skirt-like garment. The dancer's bare chest is covered with necklaces of silver and ivory, and bangles of beaten silver are worn on the arm. The dance is accompanied by drummers who beat out complex rhythms on the geta bera, a double-ended drum.

genres.name: Low-country drumming
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Low Country (Pahatha Rata) drumming encompasses the ritual percussion traditions of the southern and coastal lowlands of Sri Lanka, distinct from the Kandyan Udarata style. The principal drums include the yak bera (devil dance drum) and davula. The tradition is closely associated with tovil healing ceremonies and kolam masked theater, performed to propitiate demons or mark rites of passage. Hereditary drummers and ritual specialists maintain the tradition in villages along the southern coast.

sources.citation: Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

image.title: The Low Country "Garayak" dance
image.creator: Iamironviper
image.attribution: Iamironviper, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts:
This is performance of Sri Lankan traditional dance called the low country "Garayak" dance. Low country garayak dance is a traditional dance form that originated in the southern coastal region of Sri Lanka. It is a highly rhythmic and energetic dance that is performed to the beats of a unique drum called "gara yak bera."
The dance is typically performed by a group of male dancers who wear colorful costumes and masks. The costumes are designed to represent various characters such as demons, animals, and humans. The masks are made of wood and are intricately carved to depict the character being portrayed.

This video was recorded in the final procession of the annual Esala Festival of the historic Ruhunu Kataragama Maha Temple which was held on 11th August 2022 with the participation of a large number of devotees.

image.title: Türkülerin Başına Gelenler Politik-İdeolojik Sebeplerle Değiştirilen Türküler Üzerine
image.creator: Mustafa Dinç
image.attribution: Mustafa Dinç, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts:
Abstract
Folk songs are common examples of folk poetry in many areas of social life and are said in almost every subject. As a result of this prevalence, folk songs, which perform many overt or secret functions in line with all the functions of folklore products, have been used to reflect political-ideological ideas from time to time and even some or all of their lyrics have been changed for this purpose. In Turkey, folk songs, which have been restructured by right or left political ideologies, have been used as a propaganda tool in times of intense political activity or in election squares. In the study, which briefly emphasized the political and social conditions of the folk tradition in our country since the second half of the twentieth century, it was determined that it was replaced by political-ideological purposes by the performers who belonged to different ideological trends, especially from the 60s until today. were compared with their performances and repertoire records, and then the ways in which these changes were made were discussed. In this respect, it was determined that these changes were made in the sample folk songs, which were used as arguments of some political movements in various periods by making significant changes to their lyrics for political-ideological reasons, in the form of secularizing, conservationizing, articulating current ideological jargon to the verbal texture of the folk songs and adapting new lyrics to the melodic structure of the The study also required that this situation be considered completely separate from the concepts of variant or version.; it was concluded that it would be more accurate to consider the above practices as a censorship or adaptation.
Keywords

folk song, politics, ideology, censorship, adaptation

image.title: Bekir Sıdkı Sezgin’e Âit Muhayyer Sümbüle Ayin-i Şerifi’nin Biçim Özellikleri Açısından Tahlîli
image.creator: Sitki AKARSU
image.attribution: Sitki AKARSU, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts:
Mevlevi literatüründe Ayin-i Şerif olarak geçen formlar, günümüzde Mevlevi Ayini olarak da ifade edilmektedir. Sözlerine “Nutk-ı şerif” denilen Ayin-i şeriflerin güfteleri, Farsça’dır. Sözlerinde de, Allah’ın, peygamberin ve tarikat pirlerinin isimleri zikredilmektedir. Türk musikisi açısından da ayrı ve önemli bir yeri olan bu formlar, müzikal yönü ve anlam bütünlüğü olarak her zaman üst düzey bir besteciliğin ürünü olmuştur. Bölümleri olan “Selam” kısımları bile ayrı manaları içeren belirli temalardaki sözlerden meydana gelmiştir. Yaklaşık 160’ın üzerinde yazılmış olan Ayin-i Şeriflerden biri de, Bekir Sıdkı Sezgin tarafından bestelenmiş olan, Muhayyer Sümbüle Ayin-i Şerif’idir.
Yapılan bu çalışmada, Muhayyer Sümbüle Ayin-i Şerif’i biçim özellikleri yönü ile incelenmiş, belirli bulgulara ulaşılmıştır. Nitel araştırma yöntemlerinden, betimsel tarama modelindeki bu çalışmada, Gülçin Yahya Eser Tahlîli Yöntemi kullanılmıştır. Bu tahlil yöntemi ile Âyine ait usûl, ölçü, cümle, bölüm, makam ve güfte yapılarını gösteren eser kurgusu ile icrâ akışı tabloları verilmiş ayrıca açıklanmıştır. Yapılan çalışmadaki Ayin-i şerifin “Selam” olarak nitelendirilen kısımları da, eserin bölümlerini oluşturmaktadır. Ayin-i şerifler 4 selamdan oluştuğundan, eser de 4 bölümden oluşmaktadır. Bu bölümlerdeki usuller de, ayinlerde tercih edilen usullerden seçilmiştir. I. Selamda Devr-i Revân usulü(14/8), II. Selamda Mevlevî Evferi olarak ta nitelendirilen Ağır Evfer(9/4), III. Selamda Devr-i Kebir(28/4), Aksak Semai(10/8) ve Yürük Semâî(6/8) ile IV. Selamda da yine Ağır Evfer usûlleri kullanılmıştır. Bu 4 bölümde toplam 32 müzik cümlesi tespit edilmiştir. Muhayyer sümbüle Ayin-i şerifi, birbirinden farklı 32 müzik cümlesinden meydana gelmiştir. Bestekar sayın Sezgin, eserinde cümle içlerindeki mısralara bağlı dönüşlerdeki ezgi kalıpları hariç(bu da aynı müzik cümlesi değil, kendi içerisindeki dönüş melodileridir) hep farklı müzik cümleleri tercih etmiştir. Bu tercih, eseri olabildiğine zenginleştirmiş ve müzik cümlelerinde farklı makam geçkileri yaparak Ayin-i şerifi muazzam bir yapıya kavuşturmuştur. Ayin-i şeriflerde Mesnevi-i Şerif’ten, Divân-ı Kebîr’den ve Ahmed Eflâkî Dede’den alınan sözler dışında, lafızlar ve lafzi terennümler kullanılmıştır. Çalışma sonucunda, Muhayyer Sümbüle Ayin-i Şerif’inin toplamda 251 ölçüden oluştuğu belirlenmiştir. Ayrıca eser içerisinde bestekârın birçok makama atıf ve geçki yaptığı tespit edilmiştir.

image.depicts: Le Gèlèdé, Gèlèdè, ou Guèlèdé, est une cérémonie pratiquée par la communauté Yoruba-Nago établie dans la région Yoruba-Nago au Bénin, au Nigeria et au Togo. Des chants en langue yoruba, de la musique par quatre tambours et des danses masquées ont lieu à la fin des récoltes, et lors d'événements importants comme certaines naissances, certains décès, et mariages ou en cas de sécheresse ou d'épidémie. genres.name: Gumbe
genres.kind: drum, dance-music genre and social context (terminology contested)
genres.note: Gumbe in Guinea-Bissau is a binary dance rhythm and the country's defining popular music tradition, traced to the trans-Atlantic return of Jamaican Maroon communities to Freetown, Sierra Leone, c. 1800, from where it diffused along West African trade routes. The Guinea-Bissauan variant is played on the tina, a water drum made from a halved calabash floating in a tub and struck with closed fists; the gumbe rhythm migrated to this instrument from the original square frame drum. Crioulou, the Creole lingua franca of Guinea-Bissau, is the language of gumbe performance, making it inherently inter-ethnic and a symbol of Creole identity against colonial rule. Gumbe has been prevalent in popular music since the 1970s when bands such as Cobiana Djazz and Super Mama Djombo began mixing electric guitars with gumbe rhythms and folk traditions.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

image.depicts:
MAK Yong adalah seni tradisi Melayu yang menggabungkan unsur tari dan musik (disertai nyanyian pelakonnya), serta tutur cerita. Kesenian ini dimulai dengan ritus sakral yang disebut upacara ‘buka tanah’ dan diakhiri dengan ritual serupa. Mak Yong konon berasal dari Nara Yala, daerah Patani (saat ini masuk wilayah Thailand Selatan). Dari sana, kesenian itu kemudian menyebar ke Kelantan (Malaysia) sekitar 200 tahun yang lalu. Dari Kelantan, Mak Yong lantas masuk Singapura, kemudian menyeberang ke Riau, Indonesia. Kisah Mak Yong di Indonesia menarik untuk ditelaah dan dipelajari sebagai warisan budaya tak benda yang memperlihatkan keterkaitan budaya Melayu di tiga negara berbeda.
Banyak kisah disampaikan mengenai asal dan makna Mak Yong, dari kisah yang sifatnya sakral, dongeng, hingga ke pemaparan akademis dari para ahli. Jeanne Cuisinier dalam Dances Magiques de Kelantan (1931), misalnya, mengartikan Mak Yong sebagai roh leluhur (Mo Yang ‘nenek’ dan Po Yang ‘datuk’). Menurutnya, Mak Yong berasal dari Main Puteri, yaitu sejenis upacara pengobatan yang dilakukan dengan iringan tarian dan nyanyian. Adapun Walter William Skeat dalam Malay Magic Being: An Introduction to the Folklore and Popular Religion of the Malay Peninsula (1967) berpendapat, Mak Yong berasal dari kata Mak Hiang yang berarti roh ibu atau roh padi.
Mak Yong bersifat sakral karena pada setiap pertunjukannya diawali dan diakhiri dengan ritual ‘buka tanah’ dan ‘tutup tanah’ yang dilakukan oleh seorang bomoh, orang yang khusus memiliki keahlian dalam bidang supranatural. Para pemain, termasuk di dalamnya para pemusik dan penari, diberi air dan mantra yang dipercaya dapat membuat mereka bermain dengan baik. Semua peralatan yang dipakai dalam pementasan juga diberi mantra. Secara khusus, pemeran utama, topeng, dan peralatan musik berupa gendang dan rebab diberi lagi mantra dan jimat lain. Pada upacara buka tanah, bomoh meminta izin dan minta maaf kepada para leluhur. Selama upacara ini berlangsung, tidak boleh ada seorang pun yang melintas di depan arena pertunjukan karena dikhawatirkan mengganggu ‘yang tidak kelihatan’. Setelah upacara ini selesai, lagu Menghadap Rebab dengan tari Ular Sawah dipertunjukkan. Kemudian cerita Mak Yong dimulai dengan lagu pembukaannya, Betabik. Cerita ditampilkan melalui dialog para tokoh dan lagu-lagu yang dinyanyikan dengan iringan musik dan tarian. Pada akhir pertunjukan, bomoh akan menutupnya dengan upacara ritual yang biasa disebut upacara ‘tutup panggung’.

genres.name: Azerbaijani-language rap
genres.note: Azeri-language hip-hop emerged with the group Dəyirman, whose 2000 debut album Azərimeyk fused Azeri folk songs with rap verses. Their 2001 album Qurd contained the nationalist anthem 'Ya Qarabağ, Ya Ölüm,' which established rap as a vehicle for political commentary in Baku. Rappers perform in Azeri rather than Russian as an assertion of post-Soviet national identity; lyrics included in the national school curriculum.

genres.name: Meyxana
genres.note: Meyxana is an Azerbaijani oral poetry genre from Baku and the Absheron Peninsula in which performers improvise verses in competitive deyişmə format, using a repeating rhymed refrain (qafiyə) in 6/8 time. Suppressed as 'hooligan poetry' during the Soviet era, the form revived vigorously after independence in 1991; professional meyxanaçılar now perform at weddings and on television competitions. Since the 1990s a 'pop-meyxana' variant with electronic drums and keyboards emerged, described by Sultanova and Broughton as 'the most significant musical genre in Azerbaijan'.

genres.name: Jahrī zikr
genres.note: Jahrī zikr is documented as devotional vocal ritual. Giovanni De Zorzi reports fieldwork in 2002–2003 on a particular jahrī zikr adaptation in Turkistan and Almaty, including young devotees and an Almaty-based ensemble; the chapter frames this as a specific Sufi practice.

genres.name: Kazakh popular song
genres.note: Kazakh popular song (or 'mass song') is a genre of lyrical Kazakh-language songs created by amateur composers (halyk kompozitory or aueskoy kompozitory) combining Kazakh oral-poetic and melodic traditions with European tonal harmony; the style formed in the 1920s–1930s and reached its golden age between the 1960s and 1990s. In the 2011 national '100 Kazakh songs' competition, 59 of the top 100 were amateur compositions, demonstrating the genre's enduring dominance in Kazakh popular musical culture. The dombra remains its primary accompanying instrument alongside accordion and guitar.

sources.citation: Razia Sultanova and Megan Rancier, eds., Turkic Soundscapes: From Shamanic Voices to Hip-Hop, Routledge, 2018.

genres.name: Turan ensemble
genres.note: Turan is a Kazakh folk ensemble of traditional instruments (dombra, qyl-qobyz, sybyzgy, zhetygen, and jaw harp) whose staged pieces such as Kazakh Eli and Baqsy use nomadic and shamanic imagery for an urban audience. Megan Rancier documented a spring 2008 concert at the Kurmangazy Kazakh National Conservatory in Almaty, and a reviewed photograph shows the ensemble performing in Paris on 1 October 2014. The 2018 chapter treats the group as a contemporary post-Soviet practice; it does not give a formation year or a disbanding date.

sources.citation: Megan Rancier, 'Ancient roots, modern nation-building: Kazakh spirituality and identity in the music of the Turan ensemble', in Razia Sultanova and Megan Rancier (eds.), Turkic Soundscapes: From Shamanic Voices to Hip-Hop, Routledge, 2018, printed pp. 214–230.

genres.name: Pinn peat
genres.note: Pinpeat is the Khmer court orchestra — roneat xylophone, gong circle, drums, flute, and sralai oboe — that accompanies classical dance. Observers in 1906 described the dance as unchanged since the seventh century, and the Khmer court tradition is tied to the empire of 802–1431. Princess Norodom Buppha Devi revived it in the 1960s. The Khmer Rouge years 1975–1979 killed most classical performers. The 1999 Rough Guide reports the Phnom Penh School of Arts training again, with about a thousand students.

sources.citation: John Clewley, 'Cambodia: heavenly dancers', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides, 2000, book pp. 20–23.

image.depicts: Een kleine dame met zachte ogen en een magische stem, uit een dorpje dicht bij het legendarische Samarkand. Ze leerde de oude traditionele liederen van haar moeder en zong samen met haar op huwelijksfeesten, rituelen, oogstfeesten. Alle populaire Oezbeekse muziek werd haar van kleins af aan bijgebracht. Op de radio werd ze geconfronteerd met de klassieke muziek van meesters als Barno Eshagova. Matlubeh schreef vlijtig de teksten over en leerde ook dit repertoire. Gesteund door haar moeder die haar kinderen maar wat graag een muziekcarrière zag beginnen, trok ze naar het conservatorium waar ze het geluk had te werken met Aref Khan Hatemov en Turgun Alimatov, twee grootmeesters van de klassieke Oezbeekse muziek. Zij hebben Matlubeh muzikaal gevormd. Al snel werd zij een vaste waarde in haar land. Ze maakt deel uit van het Ensemble Shashmaqam van de nationale radio. De nationale televisie maakte een documentaire over haar carrière. De oorsprong van de muziek in Oezbekistan gaat terug tot de vierde eeuw vóór onze tijdrekening. Niet alleen in teksten maar ook in archeologische opgravingen vinden we bewijzen terug van een rijke muzikale traditie die deel uitmaakte van deze oude beschaving. genres.name: Persian pop music

genres.name: Aitysh/Aitys

Competitions are held in village and urban contexts and televised nationally; the form is considered one of the most vibrant living oral traditions of Central Asia. UNESCO inscribed Aitysh/Aitys on its Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2015.

genres.name: Balwo
genres.note: Balwo is a Somali-language music-and-poetry style documented in Djibouti and Somalia. The 1940s marker follows accounts of Abdi Sinimo's early compositions; country shading represents cross-border practice, not exclusive origin or uniform popularity.

sources.citation: Mohamed Diriye Abdullahi, Culture and Customs of Somalia, Greenwood Press, 2001.
The Life, Music and Literary Compositions of the Late Abdillahi Qarshe, 1998.

associated_areas.note: Somalia is part of Balwo's documented Somali-language practice area. Approximate prominence end; not an extinction claim. Later source/date wording includes the 2000s; the display window is conservatively capped at four decades.

sources.citation: Mohamed Diriye Abdullahi, Culture and Customs of Somalia, Greenwood Press, 2001.

genres.name: Guayla
genres.note: Guayla is documented as Eritrean popular music and dance rooted in Tigrinya practice, with a related scene in northern Ethiopia. The 1960s is a prominence anchor, not an origin claim.

sources.citation: Dexter Gordon Bryan Story, Guayla Nation: Unyielding Tigrinya Music, Dance and Identity in Eritrea, University of California dissertation, 2025.
Diplomacy, Resistance and Jazz: Twentieth Century Meetings between Ethiopian and African American Music, University of California dissertation, 2018.

associated_areas.note: The source identifies northern Ethiopia; the uniform north overlay is directional, not an administrative boundary. Approximate prominence end; not an extinction claim. Later source/date wording includes the 2020s; the display window is conservatively capped at four decades.

sources.citation: Dexter Gordon Bryan Story, Guayla Nation: Unyielding Tigrinya Music, Dance and Identity in Eritrea, University of California dissertation, 2025.

genres.name: Haul music
genres.note: Haul is a Sahrawi/Hassaniya music-and-poetry system documented across Western Sahara and Mauritania. Its source describes it as precolonial, so 1900 is only the atlas display floor, not an origin date.

sources.citation: Luis Gimenez Amoros, ‘Beyond Nationhood: Haul Music from a Postcolonial Perspective in Western Sahara and Mauritania,’ African Music 11(2), 2020, pp. 41–59, DOI 10.21504/amj.v11i2.2313.
Luis Gimenez Amoros, research on Haul and Sahrawi refugee musical identity.

associated_areas.note: Mauritania is explicitly included in the scholarly study of Haul; the layer does not claim uniform countrywide practice. Approximate prominence end; not an extinction claim. Later source/date wording includes the 2020s; the display window is conservatively capped at four decades.

sources.citation: Luis Gimenez Amoros, ‘Beyond Nationhood: Haul Music from a Postcolonial Perspective in Western Sahara and Mauritania,’ African Music 11(2), 2020.

genres.note: Dinka song traditions include ox songs, initiation songs, hymns, war songs and personally composed songs used for memory, social commentary and communication. genres.name: Cantopop
genres.note: Cantopop is Hong Kong's Cantonese-language popular song genre, emerging in the mid-1970s and reaching its global peak in the 1980s–1990s with the 'Four Heavenly Kings' (Andy Lau, Jacky Cheung, Aaron Kwok, Leon Lai); the genre remains active, with contemporary artists such as G.E.M. and Eason Chan maintaining HKG's position as a creative centre of Chinese-language pop.

genres.kind: regional instrumental and urban music tradition
genres.note: Guangdong music in Macao developed through rural bayin ensembles, urban teahouse light music and recording-era popular tunes, and remains an organized local performance tradition. The 1900 marker is a broad historical display anchor, not an exact arrival date.

genres.kind: North Korean popular and patriotic song style
genres.note: Taejung kayo is used in North Korean discourse for post-liberation popular song and, by the 1980s, a state-mediated patriotic popular style combining Korean, Western orchestral and socialist-realist elements. genres.name: ʿAtābā and mījānā
genres.note: ʿAtābā and mījānā are paired Levantine vocal forms used in folk singing and recordings. Sources describe shared practice in Lebanon and Palestine while preserving locally specific performance histories.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

associated_areas.note: ʿAtābā and mījānā is documented as paired vocal folk genres. Identifies ʿatābā and mījānā as vocal folk genres particularly popular in Lebanon and Palestine, and describes their paired contemporary use.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Kru coastal popular music
genres.kind: coastal vocal, brass-band and guitar-based popular practice
genres.note: Kru coastal communities carried vocal and instrumental practices through maritime labor networks. The source documents coastal brass-band popularity in the late 1930s and a Liberian guitar-song recording in 1947; the southern locator is deliberately approximate.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998, chapter ‘Kru Mariners and Migrants of the West African Coast’.

genres.name: Sefela
genres.kind: Basotho migrant workers' sung poetic narrative
genres.note: Sefela sa litsamaea-naha are long musical-poetic narratives associated with Basotho migrant workers' journeys from Basutoland to South African mines. A documented Lesotho performance in 1984 provides a later evidence anchor.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998, printed p. 762.

genres.name: Kundiman
genres.kind: Filipino lyrical and nationalist song genre
genres.note: Kundiman became a prominent Filipino song genre around the turn of the twentieth century, including nationalist and art-song forms. The source reports continued popularity through the American regime and Japanese occupation.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998, printed pp. 868–871.

genres.name: Bangsawan
genres.kind: Malay operatic theatre and music genre
genres.note: Bangsawan is a Malay operatic theatre and music genre established in the late nineteenth century. The Singapore chapter documents local festival and tourist performances and a 1995 museum presentation.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998, printed pp. 520–523.

genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: The Central African music survey identifies tanged harps in Chad and connects the practice zone to older Saharan harp history, including Ennedi. The northern fill is a technical regional influence zone, not an exact distribution boundary.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998, printed pp. 299–302.

genres.name: Southern Sudan harp traditions
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: The survey identifies southern Sudan among Africa's principal harp areas and discusses the Sudd as part of the older Nilo-Saharan cultural belt. The central fill is a technical regional influence zone, not a claim of uniform South Sudanese practice.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998, printed pp. 299–302.

genres.name: Marabi
genres.note: Marabi grew in Johannesburg township shebeens and dance halls as a social dance and local jazz form, combining ragtime and jazz with Black South African melodic and rhythmic practices.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 415-416.

genres.name: Kwela
genres.note: Kwela is a South African street-jazz style centered on pennywhistle melody over a repeating guitar chord pattern. It emerged in the 1940s and became a prominent recorded Black popular music.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 420-421.

genres.name: Mbaqanga
genres.note: Mbaqanga is a South African urban popular genre that emerged in the early 1960s from the marabi-based jazz tradition; the characteristic form pairs a deep-voiced male 'groaner' (simanjemanje) with a close-harmonised female chorus against electric-guitar backing, and reached its commercial peak with Mahlathini and the Mahotella Queens in the 1980s.

sources.citation: Angela Impey, 'Popular Music in Africa,' in Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008.

genres.name: Mbube
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Mbube is a style of Zulu male choral singing associated with workers' choirs. The name follows Solomon Linda's song 'Mbube', recorded with his Original Evening Birds.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, p. 420.

genres.name: Kwaito
genres.note: Kwaito emerged in Johannesburg-area townships around the late 1980s and 1990s. Its dance sound draws on house music at a slower tempo, with repeated samples, bass lines, and vocals.

genres.name: Dhrupad
genres.note: Dhrupad is the oldest surviving form of North Indian classical vocal music, dating to at least the 15th century. The Rough Guide (2000) describes it as 'the oldest vocal music genre still performed', with major lineages continuing through the Dagar Brothers and the Mallik family of Darbhanga. Using the ancient dhrupad alap and compositions set to rhythmically complex talas, it is performed today at classical music festivals across India and internationally.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.
Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

genres.name: Khayal
genres.note: Khayal (meaning 'imagination' in Urdu) is the dominant form of North Indian classical vocal performance, described by the Rough Guide (2000) as 'the most popular classical vocal style since the 19th century'. It features elaboration of a raga through improvised passages (vistar) and composed compositions (bandish), performed with tabla accompaniment. Leading contemporary exponents include Pandit Bhimsen Joshi and Rashid Khan.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.
Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

genres.name: Karnatak Classical Music
genres.note: Carnatic classical music is the principal classical tradition of South India, centered historically in Tamil Nadu with its main hub at Madras (Chennai). The Rough Guide (2000) notes 'Indian classical music has a larger audience than ever before', with the Madras music season remaining one of the world's great annual classical music festivals. Key composers are the 18th-century Trinity (Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Syama Sastri); leading 20th-century performers include M.S. Subbulakshmi and violinist L. Subramaniam.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.
Simon Broughton and Mark Ellingham (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Vol. 2: Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides Ltd, London, 2000.

genres.name: Jaipongan
genres.kind: West Javanese popular social dance music
genres.note: Jaipongan is a West Javanese popular dance developed during the 1970s from Sundanese dance movements alongside other influences. Choreographer Gugum Gumbira established studios that spread the form.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Kecak
genres.note: Kecak is a Balinese choral theater in which a large male chorus voices interlocking syllables and evokes a gamelan. Its Ramayana scenes grew from earlier trance-dance practice.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Maninka Praise Singing (Mansareh Bolo)
genres.note: Maninka praise singing in northern Sierra Leone is performed by specialist jelilu, who combine spoken praise, song, and instrumental patterns. Performances can invoke lineage history and public social obligations.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Koranko Praise Singing
genres.note: Koranko praise singing in northern Sierra Leone belongs to specialist jeli performance. A singer may begin with a familiar song or an instrumental pattern, then combine music with praise and advice.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Maringa
genres.note: Maringa is a Sierra Leonean popular guitar music rooted in the gumbe frame-drum tradition brought by freed enslaved people to Freetown; Ebenezer Calendar (1912-1985) recorded approximately 300 maringa songs from the 1950s onward, establishing the genre internationally, and it remains a living form alongside derived styles such as milo-jazz and asiko.

sources.citation: Rachel Jackson, 'The trans-atlantic journey of Gumbe: where and why has it survived,' Journal of International Library of African Music, 2012.

genres.name: Zar Healing Ceremony
genres.note: Zar is a spirit-possession healing practice documented in Ethiopia and Sudan. Music and dance are used within ceremonies for people understood to be affected by spirits.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Falasha (Beta Israel) Liturgical Music
genres.note: Falasha liturgical music is the sacred song tradition of the Beta Israel people, historically concentrated in the Gondar and Simien regions of northwestern Ethiopia.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Tina
genres.note: The tina is a water drum central to Guinea-Bissauan gumbe: it consists of a halved calabash floating in a tub of water, struck with closed fists. The transposition of the gumbe rhythm from its original square frame drum to the tina mirrors the Bahamian goombay's adoption of cylindrical drums — a local modernisation of a pre-existing rhythm onto available instruments. As both instrument and rhythmic genre name, tina is inseparable from Guinea-Bissauan Creole musical identity; Manecas Costa's 2003 album Paraiso de Gumbé features the tina/gumbe rhythm alongside the broska style of the Balanta ethnicity.

sources.citation: Rachel Jackson, 'The Trans-Atlantic Journey of Gumbé: Where and Why Has It Survived?' Journal of International Library of African Music, 2011.

genres.name: Tinga
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Tinga is a traditional music and dance form from Guinea-Bissau, documented across the country without specific concentration in one geographic area.

genres.name: Balanta brosca
genres.note: Balanta brosca is a musical style of the Balanta ethnicity, one of Guinea-Bissau's largest ethnic groups. The broska rhythm and style is documented as a distinct tradition alongside gumbe in the country's popular music landscape; Manecas Costa's 2003 album Paraiso de Gumbé features the gumbe rhythm mixed with the broska style, illustrating how Guinea-Bissauan artists blend Creole and Balanta traditions.

sources.citation: Rachel Jackson, 'The Trans-Atlantic Journey of Gumbé: Where and Why Has It Survived?' Journal of International Library of African Music, 2011.

genres.name: Kussunde
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Kussunde is a ceremonial music associated with the Balanta and coastal southern communities of Guinea-Bissau, popularized by musicians from the southern heartland.

genres.name: Som Kundere
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Som kundere is the distinctive music of the Bijagós Islands, an archipelago off the western coast of Guinea-Bissau, tied to local initiation and ceremonial life.

genres.name: Tajik popular music
genres.note: Tajik popular music is an urban song genre that developed under Soviet cultural institutions and re-emerged with new forms following independence in 1991, blending Persian-language lyrical traditions with synthesiser-driven arrangements; it remains distinct from the classical Shashmaqam tradition practised in Bukhara and Samarkand.

genres.name: Bakhshi
genres.kind: oral epic and lyric performance tradition
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Bakhshi are itinerant poet-singers of the Turkmen epic tradition found across all Turkmenistan, without fixed regional concentration.

sources.citation: Music of Central Asia: Further Reading, Listening, and Viewing, official companion, 2017, musicofcentralasia.org.

genres.name: Mukamlar
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Turkmen mukamlar (maqam suites) are classical compositions associated with the Pendi region school near the Afghan border in southern Turkmenistan.

genres.name: Hadhra
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Hadhrami music is the traditional vocal and oud tradition of the Hadhramaut Valley in eastern Yemen, historically spread along Indian Ocean trade routes.

genres.name: Adeni music
genres.kind: popular music genre / port city cosmopolitan music
genres.note: Adeni music is the distinctive coastal song tradition of Aden in southern Yemen, combining Gulf, African, and Indian Ocean influences in the historic port city.

genres.name: Yemeni hip-hop
genres.note: Yemeni hip-hop emerged from the Sanaa youth scene in the 2000s, combining Arabic lyrical traditions with American and Gulf hip-hop production styles.

genres.name: Wákà
genres.note: Wáká is a Yoruba Muslim song genre adopted from the Hausa, performed predominantly by women; first commercial recordings appeared in Lagos in the late 1920s, and professional specialists emerged after 1945; Queen Salawa Abeni (b. 1965) is the genre's contemporary superstar.

sources.citation: Christopher A. Waterman, 'Yoruba Popular Music,' in Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008.

genres.name: Sákárà
genres.note: Sákárà is a Yoruba Muslim genre of social dancing and praise, with the sákárà frame drum as its defining instrument; examples were performed in Ibadan and Lagos during or soon after World War I (1914–1918), and its golden age was the 1940s through 1960s with artists including Abibu Oluwa and Yusufu Ọlatunji.

sources.citation: Christopher A. Waterman, 'Yoruba Popular Music,' in Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008.

genres.name: Afrobeats
genres.note: Afrobeats is an umbrella for contemporary popular sounds associated with Nigeria, Ghana, and their diasporas. It developed during the 2000s and 2010s through combinations of several West African styles.

genres.name: Àpàlà
genres.note: Àpàlà originated in the Ìjẹbu area of Yorubaland probably in the early 1940s, growing out of gángan talking-drum performance; it became the dominant genre of popular music among Yoruba Muslims in the 1960s and 1970s, and its golden age was the 1950s with Haruna Ìşola and Ọmọwura as its brightest stars.

sources.citation: Christopher A. Waterman, 'Yoruba Popular Music,' in Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008.

genres.name: Dondang Sayang
genres.note: Dondang Sayang is a Malay sung-poetry tradition practiced by several Melaka communities. Two singers exchange four-line verses over violin, gong, and tambourine accompaniment.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Zapin
genres.kind: Malay-Arab social dance and music genre
genres.note: Zapin is a Malay dance-music form that originated in Johor in southern peninsular Malaysia, combining Middle Eastern melodic patterns with local rhythmic dance.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Dikir Barat
genres.note: Dikir barat is a secular group-singing form of northeastern Malaysia. A soloist opens with an improvised passage, then a seated men's chorus answers in measured rhythm with clapping and gestures.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Gabaye
genres.note: Gabaye is a ceremonial poetry and song tradition shared by both the Afar and Issa-Somali communities of Djibouti, practiced across the country.

genres.name: Afar wedding and praise songs
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Afar wedding praise songs are a vocal tradition from the Afar-inhabited territory of northern Djibouti, sung by women in call-and-response form at marriage ceremonies.

genres.name: Djibouti modern fusion
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Djibouti modern fusion blends Afar, Somali, and Arab musical influences produced by urban artists in Djibouti city, forming a nationally broadcast popular style.

genres.name: Min'yō
genres.note: Min'yō encompasses regional Japanese folk-song traditions, including Tsugaru mountain songs, Tokushima's Awa-odori songs, Miyagi fishing songs, and Okinawan repertories.

sources.citation: Smithsonian Folkways, Japan: Semiclassical and Folk Music, UNESCO Collection UNES08016, 1974, liner notes, pp. 4–6.

genres.name: Shamisen music
genres.note: Shamisen music includes several Japanese schools and styles played on the three-stringed lute. Naga-uta shamisen accompanies Kabuki dance drama.

sources.citation: Smithsonian Folkways, Japan: Semiclassical and Folk Music, UNESCO Collection UNES08016, 1974, liner notes, pp. 2–3.

genres.name: Koto music
genres.note: Japanese koto music includes solo playing that developed during the seventeenth century and later ensemble styles with increasingly elaborate overlapping parts.

sources.citation: Smithsonian Folkways, Japan: Semiclassical and Folk Music, UNESCO Collection UNES08016, 1974, liner notes, pp. 3–4.

genres.name: Shakuhachi music
genres.note: Shakuhachi music includes repertories transmitted through Japanese schools such as Kinko. The bamboo-flute piece 'Shika no Tone' is a prominent example of that school.

sources.citation: Smithsonian Folkways, Japan: Semiclassical and Folk Music, UNESCO Collection UNES08016, 1974, liner notes, p. 4.

genres.name: Kabuki music
genres.note: Kabuki music encompasses the instrumental and vocal accompaniment of Japanese theatrical dance drama. Naga-uta shamisen repertory is one documented form within it.

sources.citation: Smithsonian Folkways, Japan: Semiclassical and Folk Music, UNESCO Collection UNES08016, 1974, liner notes, pp. 2–3.

genres.name: Kayōkyoku
genres.note: Kayōkyoku is a Japanese commercial popular-song form that joined Western harmony with Japanese lyrical themes and shaped later J-pop. It was especially prominent from the 1920s through the 1980s.

genres.name: Enka
genres.note: Enka is a Japanese popular-song style that combines Japanese pentatonic melodies with Western harmonic elements. Songs often address longing, love, loss, and nostalgia.

genres.name: J-Pop
genres.note: J-pop names Japanese popular music that entered the country's mainstream in the 1990s, following earlier kayōkyoku. Its lineage includes Japanese music alongside international pop and rock influences.

genres.name: Adai-adai
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Adai-adai is a Bruneian coastal work-song tradition associated with fishing and other labor around the shore. Its performance belongs to the country's inherited local repertory.

genres.name: Jipin / Zapin
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Jipin is a Malay courtly dance-music tradition practiced across Brunei's coastal Malay communities, with origins in Riau Malay culture.

genres.name: Aduk-Aduk
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Aduk-aduk is a Bruneian communal performance associated with harvest ceremonies in interior communities. Percussion and collective participation are central to the practice.

genres.name: Likurai
genres.note: Likurai is a women's victory drum dance from Timor-Leste, documented most specifically in Suai district of Covalima province in the western part of the country.

genres.name: Ah-ahk (Korean Court Music)
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Korean court music includes repertories used at court and in Confucian ceremonies, played by orchestras with stone, metal, silk-string, and bamboo instruments.

sources.citation: Local dossier source; see private evidence record.
Local dossier source; see private evidence record.

genres.name: Farmers' songs
genres.note: Korean farmers' songs accompanied field work and expressed labor, hope, and thanksgiving. A 1951 recording documents a farmers' song drawn from the Chunhyang repertory.

sources.citation: Smithsonian Folkways, Folk and Classical Music of Korea, FW04424, 1951, liner notes, p. 3.

genres.name: Kayageum Sanjo
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Kayageum sanjo is Korean solo music for the twelve-stringed kayageum zither. A performance develops musical material through contrasting tempos.

sources.citation: Smithsonian Folkways, Korea: Vocal and Instrumental Music, UNESCO Collection UNES08010, 1965, liner notes, p. 4.

genres.name: Changga
genres.note: Changga comprises Korean songs using Western-style musical structures and sometimes adapted foreign melodies. It served educational and patriotic purposes around the late Joseon and colonial periods.

genres.name: K-pop
genres.note: K-pop is South Korean popular music shaped by the idol-group production system that developed in the 1990s. Its commercial reach expanded internationally in the 2010s.

genres.name: Modern school songs
genres.note: Modern Chinese school songs placed Chinese lyrics over adapted foreign melodies in Western diatonic style. They spread secular Western-style music through educational institutions.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music: Modernization and Globalization, 1927 to the Present, Routledge, 2023.

genres.name: Red songs
genres.note: Red songs are Chinese revolutionary and state-supported songs that were especially prominent under Mao. Later performances also revisit this repertory through nostalgia and popular culture.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music, Indiana University Press, 2020.

genres.name: Sent-down youth songs
genres.note: Sent-down youth songs were made clandestinely by urban Chinese youth displaced to rural areas during the Cultural Revolution. Their guitar-accompanied repertory drew on Chinese and foreign folk songs.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music, Indiana University Press, 2020.

genres.name: Liuxing/Tongsu music
genres.note: Liuxing/tongsu music (流行/通俗音乐) is the broad Chinese-language popular song tradition that developed in mainland China from the 1980s following Deng Xiaoping's reforms; initially absorbing Hong Kong and Taiwan pop influences, it evolved through the 1990s to encompass ballads, dance-pop, and Chinese-Wind fusion, and remains the dominant popular music category in China.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music: Modernization and Globalization, 1927 to the Present, Routledge, 2023.
Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music, Routledge, 2023.

genres.name: Chinese rock
genres.note: Chinese rock emerged in Beijing in the mid-1980s, consolidated by Cui Jian's 1986 performance of 'Nothing to My Name' (一无所有) at a national TV concert; the genre developed through Western-influenced bands such as Tang Dynasty (whose 1992 album fused hard rock with Jingju and classical Chinese elements) and remains a significant strand of Chinese popular culture today.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music, Indiana University Press, 2020.
Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music, Routledge, 2023.

genres.name: Chinese hip-hop
genres.note: Chinese-language rap emerged in the late 1980s — Harlem Yu (Taiwan, 1987) and Cui Jian (China, 1989) produced the earliest mainstream rap songs; by the 1990s Dou Wei and Chang Yusheng were blending rap with Chinese folk elements, and in the 2010s a younger generation of mainland hip-hop artists brought the genre to TV audiences through competition formats.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music, Indiana University Press, 2020.
Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music, Routledge, 2023.

genres.name: Gharnatī
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Gharnatī is the western Algerian school of North African Andalusian music. Its repertory belongs to the nubah suite tradition carried and reshaped across the Maghrib.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

associated_areas.start_label: No year is named in the note
associated_areas.note: The Rough Guide says gharnati is played mainly in Algeria, with two important Moroccan centres: Rabat, and Oujda near the Algerian border.

sources.citation: World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 1 (1999), Morocco chapter, Gharnati section, book p. 570.

genres.name: Sanʿa (Algerian Andalusian)
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Sanʿa is the Algiers school of Arab-Andalusian music. It preserves a local branch of the North African nubah song-cycle tradition.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Arab-Andalusian Nubah (Algeria)
genres.note: Algerian nubah music is an Arab-Andalusian suite tradition organized around melodic and rhythmic modes. Schools in Algiers and western Algeria developed distinct local repertories.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Hawzi
genres.note: Hawzi is an Algerian urban song style derived from Arab-Andalusian music. Often sung by men in the Tell region, it sets love poetry in local dialect to simplified Andalusian melodies.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Tuareg Tende
genres.note: Tende names a Tuareg mortar drum, the music played with it, and the gathering around that performance. It accompanies camel festivals and curing ceremonies, including documented performances near Tamanrasset.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 267-271.

genres.name: Takamba
genres.note: Takamba is Tuareg popular music built around accompanied songs and instrumental solos on the tahardent lute. Its performance reached Tamanrasset, Algeria, by 1974.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 255, 271-273.

genres.name: BaAka Mabo (Hunting Dance)
genres.note: Mabo is a BaAka hunting dance whose music combines yodeled, interlocking polyphonic singing and hollow-log drums. A recorded 1988 performance documents the dance in the Central African Republic.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 369-371.

genres.name: BaAka Dingboku (Women's Dance)
genres.note: Dingboku is a BaAka women's line dance: linked performers move together while singing and clapping, without drums. Its songs can celebrate women's sexuality and mock men.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone (ed.), The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008, pp. 370-372.

genres.name: Kabosy
genres.note: Kabosy is a small plucked chordophone from Comoros, widespread across the Comorian islands without a single dominant island of practice.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Gabusi
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Gabusi is a lute tradition of the Comoros islands, with structural variants documented on both Grande Comore and Anjouan, spread across the archipelago.

genres.name: Ndzendze
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Ndzendze is a box-zither tradition from Comoros, practiced across the islands with notable masters documented on Mwali and other islands of the archipelago.

genres.name: Valiha
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: The valiha is a bamboo tube zither and the national instrument of Madagascar, with its classical repertoire centered in the highland region around Antananarivo.

genres.name: Salegy
genres.note: Salegy is an electric guitar-driven popular music from northern Madagascar, developed in the Antsiranana (Diana) region from the 1960s, characterised by a distinctive 6/8 rhythm and call-and-response vocals.

genres.name: Ba-gasy (Hiragasy)
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Hiragasy is a Malagasy highland performance tradition especially associated with Merina communities. Troupes combine music, dance, and kabary oratory in extended public spectacles or competitions.

genres.name: Kalon'ny Fahiny
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Kalon ny fahiny is the traditional classical music of the Merina people of the central highlands of Madagascar, associated with Antananarivo royal court culture.

genres.name: Nabaṭī
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Nabaṭī is the vernacular sung poetry of the Arabian Peninsula, historically associated with central Arabian Bedouin (Najd region); it serves as the text for genres such as sāmrī and ʿarḍa; anyone from shepherd to sheikh may be a nabaṭī poet, and the tradition has spread throughout the Gulf States where it remains popular today.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.
Lisa Urkevich, 'Nabaṭī,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ṣawt
genres.note: Ṣawt is the leading art music of Kuwait, Bahrain, and the upper Arabian Gulf, performed by a male vocalist accompanying himself on the ʿūd with mirwās drum support; it was developed by the Kuwaiti Abdullah Al-Farāj (1836–1901) and spread through royal and merchant patronage across the Gulf; although it began to wane in the 1970s, young Gulf musicians continue to write and perform in the genre into the 21st century.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.
Lisa Urkevich, 'Ṣawt,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Al-Samri
genres.kind: folk tradition / percussion and vocal genre
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Samri is a Hejazi pop folk tradition from the western Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia, centered in Jeddah, Mecca, and Medina.

genres.name: Bogino Duu
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Bogino duu is a Mongolian short-song form, distinguished from the long-song tradition by its comparatively brisk tempo and rhythmic character.

genres.name: Gule Wamkulu
genres.note: Gule Wamkulu is a Chewa Nyau masked ritual dance practiced in Mozambique, Malawi, and Zambia. Performances mark initiations, weddings, funerals, and the installation of chiefs.

sources.citation: UNESCO, Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity: Proclamations 2001, 2003 and 2005, 2006, p. 62.

genres.name: Marrabenta
genres.note: Marrabenta is Mozambique's most emblematic topical popular genre, developed in the 1950s in the suburban slums of Maputo (then Lourenço Marques) on three guitars fashioned from oil-tin cannisters; its basis is the indigenous majika rhythm modified with influences from ska, soul, rumba, reggae, and Brazilian percussion, and it served as a revolutionary voice for oppressed people under Portuguese rule.

sources.citation: Angela Impey, 'Popular Music in Africa,' in Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008.

genres.name: Aitys
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Aitys is a Kazakh and Kyrgyz contest of improvised spoken or sung poetry. Opposing akyns answer audience-chosen topics with wit and rhythm, accompanied in Kazakhstan by the dombra.

sources.citation: Razia Sultanova and Megan Rancier, eds., Turkic Soundscapes: From Shamanic Voices to Hip-Hop, Routledge, 2018.
Music of Central Asia: Further Reading, Listening, and Viewing, official companion, 2017, musicofcentralasia.org.
Gulnar Abdirakhman, 'Mass Music in Kazakhstan: The Phenomenon and Its Interpretation,' in Razia Sultanova, ed., Turkic Soundscapes: From Shamanic Voices to Hip-Hop, Routledge, 2018.

genres.name: Zhyrau
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Zhyrau are Central Asian singers of heroic epic poetry, accompanied by the kobyz. The tradition belongs to Kipchak-speaking cultures including communities in Kazakhstan.

genres.name: Gule Wamkulu
genres.note: Gule Wamkulu is a Chewa Nyau masked ritual dance practiced in Malawi, Mozambique, and Zambia. Performances mark initiations, weddings, funerals, and the installation of chiefs.

sources.citation: UNESCO, Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity: Proclamations 2001, 2003 and 2005, 2006, p. 62.
