genres.name: Jit
genres.note: Jit is a Zimbabwean popular music style that emerged in the 1960s from the Harare township scene, combining electric guitar with Shona musical rhythms.

genres.name: Tunisian Andalusian Music (Malouf)
genres.note: Tunisian maʾlūf is a local branch of North African Andalusian music. Its nubah suites combine sung poetry and instrumental sections through ordered melodic and rhythmic modes.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Tunisian Gnawa
genres.note: Tunisian Gnawa ceremony music accompanies possession and healing rites with singing, iron castanets, and the three-stringed gumbri lute. Annual rites honor the patron saint Sidi Marzuk.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Fūndū
genres.note: Fūndū is a Tunisian vocal form that developed by the late nineteenth century. It combines maʾlūf performance style with melodic and rhythmic material from Tunisian popular traditions.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Mizwid
genres.note: Mizwid is a Tunisian popular genre named after its characteristic double-pipe instrument; it emerged as an urban working-class dance style in the 1980s and became the most commercially successful popular genre in Tunisia by the 1990s.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Ughniyya (Tunisian)
genres.note: Al-ughniyya al-tūnisiyya is the dominant media song genre of Tunisia, an urban vocal form for solo singer, chorus and ensemble in couplet-refrain structure, derived from Arab-Andalusian maʾlūf contexts; the Rashīdiyya Institute (1934) and state radio promoted a 'golden age' of Tunisian song from the 1930s to 1960s, and contemporary stars continue to perform it across the Arab world.

sources.citation: Ruth F. Davis and Richard C. Jankowsky, 'Ughniyya (Tunisian),' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Zamrock
genres.note: Zamrock emerged in Zambia during the early 1970s, combining local musical influences with psychedelic rock, blues, and funk. Rikki Ililonga and Musi-O-Tunya were early figures in the scene.

genres.name: Kalindula
genres.note: Kalindula is Zambian popular music named for a bass instrument used in its ensembles. It combines local dance traditions with twentieth-century popular styles and homemade string and percussion instruments.

genres.name: Dansi
genres.note: Dansi is the non-Islamic popular dance-music genre that developed in Tanzania and across East Africa from the 1940s, played by guitar orchestras in Swahili and regional languages; it grew out of the beni brass-band tradition of World War I and was propelled by Nairobi and Dar es Salaam recording industries into a region-wide popular form.

sources.citation: Angela Impey, 'Popular Music in Africa,' in Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008.

genres.name: Beni / Mganda
genres.note: In Tanzania, beni became known as mganda: a processional dance style with choreographed marching and calabash-kazoo imitations of military brass bands.

sources.citation: Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 1: Africa, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: C-pop
genres.note: C-pop (Huayu liuxing gequ, 華語流行歌曲) is a pan-Chinese popular music category that first appeared as a marketing term in Hong Kong in the 1970s and encompasses all Mandarin and Cantonese popular songs produced across the Chinese-speaking world, bridging markets in HKG, Taiwan, mainland China and diaspora communities globally.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music: Modernization and Globalization, 1927 to the Present, Routledge, 2023.
Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music, Routledge, 2023.

genres.name: Zhungdra
genres.kind: classical music of local Bhutanese origin
genres.note: Zhungdra, or gzhung-sgra, is a Bhutanese music category described as locally originating, distinct from Tibetan-derived boedra and newer rigsar songs.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Boedra
genres.note: Boedra, or Bod-sgra, is Bhutanese music associated with Tibetan origins. It is distinguished locally from zhungdra and the modern rigsar style.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Jhyaure
genres.note: Jhyaure is a popular Nepali dance-song form heard in the repertory of Gaine itinerant musicians and across several of the country's musical communities.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Damai Baja
genres.note: Damai baja is an ensemble tradition of Nepal's hereditary Damai musicians. Its bands play for weddings, processions, and other life-cycle rites as both entertainment and auspicious ceremony.

sources.citation: Alison Arnold, ed., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 5: South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent, Garland Publishing, 2000.

genres.name: Adhunik Geet
genres.note: Adhunik Geet are modern Nepali songs developed in Kathmandu from the 1940s, combining classical ragas with new literary texts and Western harmonic arrangements.

sources.citation: Paul D. Greene, 'Musical media and cosmopolitanisms in Nepal's popular music, 1950–2006,' Anthem Press 2010.

genres.name: Lok Geet
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Lok Geet are Nepali folk songs spanning the hills, Terai plains, and mountain communities across the country, with no single province dominating the tradition.

genres.name: Ṣawt
genres.note: Sawt is a Gulf musical genre practiced in Muscat and the northern coastal towns of Oman, combining melodic singing with frame drum rhythms.

genres.name: Razha / Al-Razfa
genres.note: Al-Razfa is a communal performance in Oman and the United Arab Emirates. Two facing lines of men answer one another in sung chants while dancers move between them; verses often draw on Nabati poetry.

genres.name: Liwa
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Liwa is a music and dance tradition of communities of East African descent along the Batinah coast and Muscat area in northern Oman.

genres.name: Luk Thung
genres.note: Luk thung is Thai popular music that took shape in the 1940s and speaks especially to rural and migrant working-class audiences. Its songs often evoke farm life, labor, and displacement.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Li-ke
genres.note: Li-ke is a Thai street-theater tradition performed on temporary urban stages. Its music and action mix older dance-drama repertory with popular songs familiar to contemporary audiences.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Piphat
genres.note: Piphat is a Thai classical ensemble combining winds and percussion. It serves courtly, ceremonial, and theatrical music, including ritual compositions.

sources.citation: Terry E. Miller and Sean Williams, eds., The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, vol. 4: Southeast Asia, Garland Publishing, 1998.

genres.name: Stalile/Kuda
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Stalile and Kuda are ceremonial music forms of Eritrea documented among highland and lowland communities; their precise regional distribution remains under research.

genres.name: Gaeda
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Gaeda is a Tigrinya vocal tradition from the central highlands of Eritrea, performed during social gatherings and ceremonies in the Asmara region.

genres.name: MaHber Theatre Asmara music
genres.note: The Mahber Theatre of Asmara is the principal venue of Eritrean performing arts, established in the highland capital city during the early twentieth century.

genres.name: Ṣawt
genres.note: Ṣawt is an upper Gulf song tradition also performed in Qatar. Its characteristic ensemble pairs a singer playing the ʿūd with a mirwās drummer.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.
Lisa Urkevich, 'Ṣawt,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Nabaṭī
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Nabaṭī is vernacular Arabian poetry practiced in Qatar and across the Gulf. Its poems on love, praise, and tribal life are often recited or sung.

sources.citation: Richard C. Jankowsky, vol. ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.
Lisa Urkevich, 'Nabaṭī,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Küü
genres.note: Küü (plural küüs, pronounced like the first two letters of "cute") is the Kyrgyz instrumental composition tradition, primarily for komuz (three-stringed plucked lute), kyl kiyak (two-stringed bowed fiddle), or temir komuz (jew's harp). Unlike anonymous folk music, küü composers from the early 19th century are known by name and widely venerated. Each küü is programmatic — a description of natural phenomena, an inner state, or a narrative event. The literal meaning of küü is "mood," "state," or "temperament." Küüs are still actively composed and performed by contemporary akyns.

sources.citation: Tengir-Too: Mountain Music of Kyrgyzstan, Smithsonian Folkways SFW CD 40520, 2005. Liner notes by Raziya Syrdybaeva, Kyrgyz National Conservatory.

genres.name: Kabyle popular music
genres.note: Kabyle popular music is a Berber-language (Tamazight) genre from the Kabylie region of northern Algeria, pioneered by Slimane Azem (1950s–60s) and given international reach by Idir, whose 1973 single 'A Vava Inouva' sold 200,000 copies in Europe by 1978 and became the first Algerian hit on French national radio; the genre blends Amazigh melodic traditions with acoustic guitar in a style developed partly in response to state-mandated Arabization policies, and continues as a vehicle for Amazigh identity.

sources.citation: Jane E. Goodman, 'From Village to Vinyl: Genealogies of New Kabyle Song,' in Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008.

genres.name: Amapiano
genres.note: Amapiano is a South African house music sub-genre developed in Pretoria and Johannesburg townships from around 2012, characterised by piano-driven rhythm sections, log-drum bass lines and soulful vocal samples; it reached mainstream and international prominence from 2017 and became one of Africa's most exported contemporary music styles.

genres.name: Sungura
genres.note: Sungura is a Zimbabwean popular dance music genre that developed in Harare from the early 1980s, drawing on Kenyan benga guitar rhythms with driving bass lines and call-and-response vocals in Shona; it remains the most widely consumed grassroots popular genre in Zimbabwe, with Alick Macheso maintaining its commercial dominance.

genres.name: ZimDancehall
genres.note: ZimDancehall is a Zimbabwean genre fusing Jamaican dancehall rhythms with Shona and Ndebele lyrics, developed in Harare's low-income suburbs from around 2000; Soul Jah Love and Winky D established it as the voice of urban Zimbabwean youth and it subsequently gained listeners across southern Africa.

genres.name: Pandza
genres.note: Pandza is a Mozambican urban popular genre developed in Maputo in the 1990s, blending kwaito and marrabenta rhythms with local vernacular Portuguese lyrics; it emerged as the post-civil-war commercial sound of southern Mozambique and remains the dominant contemporary pop style in Maputo's entertainment industry.

genres.name: Rwandan popular music
genres.note: Contemporary Rwandan popular music (ugushake) emerged in Kigali from around 2000, combining East African dancehall, Congolese rumba and US hip-hop influences with Kinyarwanda and French lyrics; the post-genocide reconstruction era produced a commercially active scene in which artists such as Tom Close and Knowless Butera built regional followings.

genres.name: Guinean popular music
genres.note: Guinean popular music (Conakry manding pop) emerged from state-sponsored orchestras of the 1960s, grafting Mande griot melodic tradition onto Cuban son and jazz rhythms; Bembeya Jazz Nacional, Guinea's national band, became the archetype, and a continuous lineage of electric Mande pop has persisted in Conakry through contemporary artists.

genres.name: Ethio-pop
genres.note: Ethio-pop is a contemporary Ethiopian popular music genre that emerged in Addis Ababa after the fall of the Derg in 1991, synthesising Amharic lyrical traditions with electronic production, R&B and dancehall influences; Teddy Afro, Aster Aweke and Ejigayehu Shibabaw (Gigi) define its global profile alongside a large domestic music industry.

genres.name: Sinhala popular music
genres.note: Sinhala popular music is a Western-influenced vocal genre in the Sinhala language, developed from the 1960s through Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation programmes and Sinhala cinema; Nanda Malini and Sunil Edirisinghe established its lyrical ballad tradition, which continues with contemporary rock and pop productions from Colombo.

genres.name: Bangla pop
genres.note: Bangla pop is a Bangladeshi popular music genre that emerged from Dhaka's rock band scene of the 1980s, developing an acoustic-electric style distinct from Indian film music; bands such as LRB (Love Runs Blind) and James defined its sound through the 1990s, and the genre remains the dominant commercial music of Bangladesh.

genres.name: Pakistani pop music
genres.note: Pakistani pop music emerged from Karachi and Lahore from the 1970s, with Nazia Hassan's 1980 'Aap Jaisa Koi' — Pakistan's first international pop crossover — marking its commercial breakthrough; the genre synthesises Urdu lyrical traditions with Western pop production, and Coke Studio's sessions from 2008 renewed international interest in Pakistani popular forms.

genres.name: Filmi (Hindi film music)
genres.note: Filmi (Hindi film music) is the popular song genre produced for Bollywood cinema, the world's most prolific film industry; originating in Mumbai from the first Indian sound film in 1931, it blends Hindustani raga structures with Western orchestration and folk elements, with playback singers Lata Mangeshkar and Mohammed Rafi defining its golden age and A.R. Rahman modernising it from the 1990s.

genres.name: Khalīji
genres.note: Khalīji is the dominant popular song genre of the Gulf Arab states, practised across the UAE, and characterised by sawt-derived melodies, call-and-response vocal textures, and the leywah and samri rhythmic cycles; it was commercialised from the mid-1970s through cassette distribution and satellite television, and continues as a major pop form alongside Western-influenced Gulf pop.

sources.citation: Lisa Urkevich, 'Khalījī,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Khalīji
genres.note: Khalīji is the principal popular song tradition of Bahrain, sharing the Gulf-wide leywah and samri rhythmic vocabulary but with a distinctive Bahraini vocal ornamentation; Bahrain's position as an early Gulf media centre helped establish local Khalīji artists on the pan-Arab cassette market from the late 1970s.

sources.citation: Lisa Urkevich, 'Khalījī,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Khalīji
genres.note: Khalīji is Kuwait's principal popular song genre, anchored in the sawt tradition of the pearl-diving era and commercialised from the mid-1970s; Kuwaiti artists helped define the pan-Gulf cassette style through TV variety programmes on Kuwait Television and remain prominent on the contemporary streaming scene.

sources.citation: Lisa Urkevich, 'Khalījī,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Khalīji
genres.note: Khalīji is the dominant popular song form of Qatar, practised in the shared Gulf musical idiom; Qatar's small population has meant most prominent Qatari performers work across the pan-Gulf market, and the genre is sustained through state-supported music institutions and Al Jazeera-era satellite broadcasting.

sources.citation: Lisa Urkevich, 'Khalījī,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

genres.name: Syrian popular song
genres.note: Syrian popular song is an Arabic-language urban vocal genre that consolidated in Damascus and Aleppo from the 1970s, combining Egyptian-influenced orchestral arrangements with Syrian maqam ornamentation; artists such as George Wassouf and Asala Nasri achieved pan-Arab popularity, and the scene continues across diaspora communities following the 2011 conflict.

genres.name: Modern Iraqi song
genres.note: Modern Iraqi song is a Baghdad-centred popular vocal genre distinct from the classical maqam tradition, emerging in the 1950s through radio and cinema; Nazem Al-Ghazali brought international prominence to the form, and Kadim Al Saher later developed it into pan-Arab pop with literary Arabic lyrics, maintaining a substantial audience across the Middle East and diaspora.

genres.name: Georgian popular music
genres.note: Georgian popular music is a post-Soviet urban genre that emerged following independence in 1991, blending Georgian polyphonic vocal tradition with Western pop, rock, and electronic influences; Tbilisi-based artists compete in Eurovision and collaborate with international producers, while the city's electronic music scene has gained global recognition since the 2010s.

genres.name: Kyrgyz popular music
genres.note: Kyrgyz popular music is an urban vocal genre that developed following independence in 1991, often combining komuz-derived melodic lines with contemporary electronic production; it coexists with the epic Manas oral tradition and Soviet-era estrada (variety) song, and artists perform in both Kyrgyz and Russian for domestic and Central Asian audiences.

genres.name: Turkmen popular music
genres.note: Turkmen popular music is a state-mediated urban song form that developed following independence in 1991, merging Soviet-era estrada style with Turkmen language lyrics and dutar-inflected melodic contours; it operates largely under state broadcast oversight and is distinct from the classical bakhshi epic singing tradition, which continues among specialist practitioners.

genres.name: Mongolian popular music
genres.note: Mongolian popular music is an Ulaanbaatar-centred genre that emerged with democratisation in 1990, encompassing rock, pop, and hip-hop alongside traditional khoomei (throat singing) influences; groups like The HU have brought Mongolian rock to global audiences by fusing nomadic instruments with heavy metal, while K-pop-influenced idol pop dominates domestic charts.

genres.name: Cypriot laïkó
genres.note: Cypriot laïkó is the island's dominant popular song genre, sharing the Greek mainland laïkó tradition of orchestral bouzouki-led arrangements but with local Cypriot dialect and performance culture; Cyprus has produced internationally recognised artists who have crossed into the pan-Greek market and Eurovision, and the genre remains the primary commercial pop form in the Greek-Cypriot community.

genres.name: Gabonese popular music
genres.note: Gabonese popular music is an Afro-jazz and acoustic guitar-based genre developed in Libreville from the 1960s, drawing on Fang and Myene oral traditions alongside Congolese rumba influences; Pierre Akendengué established its international profile with French-language lyrics and acoustic arrangements, and younger artists have incorporated Afrobeat and urban contemporary styles.

genres.name: Togolese popular music
genres.note: Togolese popular music is a Lomé-centred genre that emerged in the 1970s, blending Ghanaian highlife, Congolese rumba, and local Ewe percussion traditions; Roger Damawuzan was the defining artist of the genre's formative decade, and contemporary Togolese musicians have integrated Afrobeats and urban gospel into an evolving popular scene.

genres.name: Beninese popular music
genres.note: Beninese popular music is a Cotonou-centred genre that developed from the 1960s, drawing on Fon and Yoruba rhythmic traditions, Congolese guitar styles, and Cuban-influenced big-band arrangements; Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes Band were the genre's most internationally visible act, and contemporary Beninese artists participate in the pan-West African Afrobeats scene.

genres.name: Gambian popular music
genres.note: Gambian popular music is a Banjul-centred genre that combines the Mande kora-griot tradition with Western amplification and pop arrangements; Jaliba Kuyateh is the genre's most prominent practitioner, blending griot repertoire with dance rhythms for mass audiences, and the Gambia's small size has kept its popular scene closely tied to the broader Senegambian and West African pop market.

genres.name: Sierra Leone afropop
genres.note: Sierra Leone afropop is a Freetown-centred popular genre that draws on the palm-wine guitar tradition of S.E. Rogie, Krio cultural identity, and West African highlife; post-civil-war reconstruction from 2002 brought a revived urban scene, and contemporary Sierra Leonean artists participate in the pan-African Afrobeats ecosystem while maintaining local Krio-language expression.

genres.name: Burkinabè popular music
genres.note: Burkinabè popular music is an Ouagadougou-centred field that, by the late 1990s, already mixed reggae (Black So Man), soul-funk (Georges Ouédraogo), afro-pop (Pierre Sandwidi), and Congolese-styled dance (Thomas Tiendrébéogo), while radio still favoured foreign soukous, mapouka, and zouglou. National stars named for that decade include Simporé Maurice, Traoré Amadou Ballaké, and Kaboré Roger. Rapper Smockey later established a hip-hop scene, and Victor Démé and Floby represent the subsequent acoustic and popular-song wave.

sources.citation: François Bensignor, 'Burkina Faso: hidden treasure', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 1, Africa, Europe and the Middle East, Rough Guides, 1999, book pp. 437–439.

genres.name: Botswana popular music
genres.note: Botswana popular music is a Gaborone-centred genre influenced by neighbouring South African kwaito and house music, Setswana-language praise poetry, and kwasa kwasa dance rhythms from the DRC; the country's relatively high per-capita income has sustained a domestic recording industry, and Afro-pop acts participate in the regional Southern African popular scene.

genres.name: Malawian popular music
genres.note: Malawian popular music is a Blantyre and Lilongwe-centred genre that developed from the 1970s, blending Chichewa-language lyrics with Southern African guitar styles, Congolese soukous, and reggae influences; Lucius Banda established the genre's political dimension through protest music, and contemporary Malawian artists participate in the pan-African gospel and Afrobeats markets.

genres.name: Mauritanian popular music
genres.note: Mauritanian popular music is rooted in the iggawen griot tradition of the Moorish Hassaniya-speaking community, in which hereditary musicians accompany the tidinit lute and ardin harp; Dimi Mint Abba brought this repertoire to international audiences from the 1970s, and contemporary artists such as Noura Mint Seymali integrate electronic production while maintaining Arabic-language maqam contours.

genres.name: Libyan popular music
genres.note: Libyan popular music is a Tripoli-centred Arabic-language urban song genre that developed from the 1960s under radio broadcast sponsorship, blending Egyptian-influenced maqam melody with local Libyan rhythmic styles; Hamid Al-Shaeri relocated to Cairo and became a key architect of pan-Arab synthesiser pop in the 1980s, and Libyan artists continue to circulate in the North African and Gulf Arab music markets.

genres.name: Heello
genres.note: Heello (also heelo) is the dominant modern popular song form of Somalia, emerging from the belwo lyric genre introduced around 1943-45 in Hargeysa (British Somaliland) by Cabdi Sinimo, who devised a short new poem form transmitted by radio and tape. The belwo evolved into the longer heello by circa 1948 (Period One), championed by Cabdullaahi Qarshe, then became a vehicle for independence themes in 1955-60 (Period Two), and since 1960 has continued as the primary urban song form, combining Somali oral imagery with instruments imported from abroad and disseminated via the national radio.

sources.citation: John William Johnson, 'The development of the genre heello in modern Somali poetry,' PhD dissertation, Indiana University, 1974.
John William Johnson, 'The Development of the Genre Heello in Modern Somali Poetry,' PhD dissertation, ProQuest 10672924, 2017.

genres.name: Sahrawi popular music
genres.note: Sahrawi popular music is a Hassaniya Arabic-language genre developed by communities of the Western Sahara diaspora, particularly in the Tindouf refugee camps in Algeria; it draws on tidinit lute and ardine harp traditions shared with Mauritania, and was brought to European audiences by Mariem Hassan in the 1980s–2000s, representing both cultural continuity and political expression for the Sahrawi people.

genres.name: Comorian twarab
genres.note: Comorian twarab is an archipelago-specific variant of the East African tarabu tradition, performed at weddings and social celebrations in Shikomori and Arabic, combining oud accompaniment with call-and-response vocal textures; it developed its local character through French colonial and Arab seafaring contacts, and remains the dominant popular music form alongside ngoma percussion ceremonies.

genres.name: Burundian popular music
genres.note: Burundian popular music is a Bujumbura-centred genre that developed from the 1970s alongside the famous royal drum (karyenda) tradition, blending Kirundi-language lyric forms with Congolese soukous guitar styles and East African rumba; post-2015 political instability has driven many artists into diaspora while a domestic scene continues through church-based gospel pop and youth-oriented urban music.

genres.name: Gumbé popular music
genres.note: Gumbe is Guinea-Bissau's Kriolu popular music, polyrhythmic and often compared loosely with samba, sung about daily life, Amílcar Cabral, and the independence struggle. The first Guinea-Bissau vinyl single, recorded in Portugal in 1973 by Djorcon (Ernesto Dabó), was acoustic gumbe; Cobiana Djazz, led by the poet-composer Zé Carlos, was already popular in 1972. Later electric bands including Super Mama Djombo continued the form, which the Rough Guide also calls a catch-all word for local music even while distinguishing tina, tinga, and ethnic styles.

sources.citation: Rachel Jackson, 'The trans-atlantic journey of Gumbe: where and why has it survived,' Journal of International Library of African Music, 2012.

Guus de Klein, 'Guinea-Bissau: the backyard beat of gumbe', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 1, Africa, Europe and the Middle East, Rough Guides, 1999, book pp. 499–501.

genres.name: Solomon Islands string band
genres.note: Solomon Islands string band music is an acoustic popular genre that emerged in the 1960s from Melanesian adaptations of Hawaiian guitar and ukulele styles introduced by missionaries; performed in Pijin and regional languages, it combines guitar, ukulele, and bass guitar with harmonised vocals, and remains the most distinctively Solomon Islander popular form alongside imported reggae and hip-hop.

genres.name: Contemporary famo
genres.note: Contemporary famo is the electrically amplified studio form of Lesotho's accordion-based popular genre, developed from the 1970s with electric bass and drum kit replacing traditional percussion; Puseletso Seema and later artists have released cassette and digital recordings for the Basotho diaspora market, maintaining famo's role as a vehicle for Sesotho cultural identity while modernising its production aesthetic.

genres.name: Swazi popular music
genres.note: Swazi popular music is a Mbabane-centred genre that developed from the 1990s, drawing on South African kwaito and maskandi guitar styles and performed in siSwati; the small domestic market has meant Swazi artists typically circulate across the Southern African regional scene, and afrobeats influences have become prominent in the contemporary studio sound since the 2010s.

genres.name: South Sudanese hip-hop
genres.note: South Sudanese hip-hop is a diaspora-rooted popular genre that developed in the mid-2000s, primarily in Nairobi and Western cities among South Sudanese refugees; Emmanuel Jal pioneered the form by addressing war, displacement, and reconciliation in English and Nuer, and following independence in 2011 a domestic Juba-based scene has emerged incorporating Dinka and Arabic influences.

genres.name: São Tomé puxa
genres.wikipedia_title: Music of São Tomé and Príncipe
genres.note: Puxa is the popular dance music of São Tomé and Príncipe, a Creole genre that blends African percussion, Portuguese colonial song, and Cuban and Brazilian influences; developed in São Tomé city from the 1970s post-independence era, it is performed for street celebrations alongside the older ússua and socopé rhythms, and remains the archipelago's most distinctively popular form.

genres.name: Cantopop
genres.note: Cantopop (Cantonese popular music) is the dominant popular genre of Macau, shared with Hong Kong, performed in Cantonese and marketed across the greater Guangdong and overseas Chinese diaspora; the genre consolidated in the mid-1970s through Hong Kong-produced cassettes and TV variety shows that circulated freely in Macau, and Portuguese colonial Macau developed its own small recording scene alongside the dominant Hong Kong mainstream.

genres.name: Taiwanese hip-hop
genres.note: Taiwanese funny rap, as the 1999 Rough Guide describes Jutoupi's three albums, mixes Hokkien and Mandarin accents to joke about politics and identity. His 1996 album Hexie de Yewan was built entirely from samples of aboriginal songs, the first time that material appeared on a mainstream Taiwanese record. Blacklist Studio had already put rap beside rock on Song of Madness in 1989.

sources.citation: Wang Ying-fen, 'Taiwan: from innocence to funny rap', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides, 2000, book pp. 237–239.

genres.name: Chinese Wind pop
genres.note: Chinese Wind pop (zhongguo feng, 中國風) is a Mandarin popular genre that fuses Chinese classical poetry, pentatonic melodies, and traditional instrumentation with contemporary hip-hop and R&B production; pioneered by Jay Chou (Zhou Jielun) and Wang Leehom after 2000, it became the dominant creative direction in Taiwan-produced Mandopop and circulated across Greater China and the global Chinese diaspora.

sources.citation: Ya-Hui Cheng, The Evolution of Chinese Popular Music, Indiana University Press, 2020.

genres.name: South African bubblegum
genres.note: South African bubblegum is synthesised dance-pop that rose in the mid-1980s and peaked in the late 1980s, with short call-and-response melodies, programmed drums, and a disco beat, sung in Sotho, Zulu, and Tsonga. Yvonne Chaka Chaka, Brenda Fassie, and Chicco Twala are the voices named for that decade. A second catalogue row used the same name and is merged here.

sources.citation: Angela Impey, 'Popular Music in Africa,' in Ruth M. Stone, ed., The Garland Handbook of African Music, 2nd ed., Routledge, 2008.

genres.name: Kuduro
genres.note: Kuduro is an Angolan electronic dance genre that emerged in the early 1990s in the musseques (informal settlements) of Luanda, blending house, electro, and techno beats with semba rhythms and rapid-fire Portuguese-language vocals; its name, meaning 'hard ass' in reference to the stiff-body dance style, reflects its street origins, and it gained international recognition in the late 2000s through Buraka Som Sistema's collaborations with artists worldwide.

genres.name: Turkish hip-hop
genres.note: Istanbul hip-hop is described as one of the new popular-music trends that developed rapidly in the city from the 1990s and then travelled with films and tours. The rapper Ceza is cited for adapting hip-hop to local values, and the Istanbul Style Breakers are cited as a crew of women rappers and breakdancers presenting a local style against American gangsta imagery. The same chapter's evidence is a scene survey, not a claim that hip-hop began in a single year.

sources.citation: Ivanka Vlaeva, 'Musical images of Istanbul from Fatih Akın's films and stage performances', in Razia Sultanova and Megan Rancier (eds.), Turkic Soundscapes: From Shamanic Voices to Hip-Hop, Routledge, 2018, printed pp. 114–119.

genres.name: Equatoguinean popular music
genres.note: By the late 1990s Malabo bands were working mainly in Cameroonian makossa, with soukous and rock also heard, while acoustic guitar groups from Annobón blended Spanish folk guitar with local strings and the pandero frame drum. Desmali y su Grupo Dambo de la Costa, based in Malabo, were the best-known acoustic band. In Madrid's exile suburb, Las Hijas del Sol released Sibeba in 1995, mixing Bubi a cappella singing with reggae, makossa, and bikutsi, and the Annobonese group Máscara had already had a home hit with Bi Mole in the early 1990s. Elvis Romeo, also from Annobón, was fusing rap with traditional music.

sources.citation: Manuel Domínguez, 'Equatorial Guinea: malabo blues', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 1, Africa, Europe and the Middle East, Rough Guides, 1999, book pp. 477–479.

genres.name: Djambadon
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Djambadon is a Mandinga style documented in Bissau alongside the more acoustic Kriolu forms tina and tinga and the ethnic styles kussundé, brosca, and kundere. The Rough Guide distinguishes it from gumbe, which that chapter treats both as a specific Kriolu popular beat and as a loose name for music in Guinea-Bissau. No start year or named djambadon band is given.

sources.citation: Guus de Klein, 'Guinea-Bissau: the backyard beat of gumbe', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 1, Africa, Europe and the Middle East, Rough Guides, 1999, book pp. 499–500.

genres.name: Ramkbach
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Ramkbach is the sad, high, country-style Cambodian song used for broken hearts and departures to the city. The Rough Guide calls Song Senghorn the queen of ramkbach and describes the style on her cassette Spean Sang Snai beside village ramvong. No start year and no end year are named.

sources.citation: John Clewley, 'Cambodia: heavenly dancers', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides, 2000, book p. 23.

genres.name: Lakon bassac
genres.note: Lakon bassac is Cambodia's popular theatre, created by Cambodians near the Bassac river at the turn of the twentieth century. The 1999 Rough Guide still presents it as the country's popular theatre and likens its sound to Vietnamese cai luong.

sources.citation: John Clewley, 'Cambodia: heavenly dancers', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides, 2000, book pp. 22–23.

genres.name: Gezaixi
genres.note: Gezaixi is the opera the 1999 Rough Guide calls the only genre truly native to Taiwan. Outdoor shows still mix the Japanese-period o-pe-ra-hi style of 1895–1945 with pop songs, keyboards, and drum kit. Television gezaixi produced stars such as Yang Lihua, and Ming Hua Yuan is named as the leading troupe, with five companies and its own school.

sources.citation: Wang Ying-fen, 'Taiwan: from innocence to funny rap', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides, 2000, book pp. 235–237.

genres.name: Hakka mountain song
genres.start_label: No year is named in the note
genres.note: Hakka mountain song uses three tunes fitted to the six tones of Hakka, with improvised texts and public contests. The Rough Guide says the songs are still taught and contested. The same chapter's best-known Hakka instrumental bayin group is the Chen family troupe of Miaoli, led by Zheng Rongxing. No start year and no end year are named.

sources.citation: Wang Ying-fen, 'Taiwan: from innocence to funny rap', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides, 2000, book p. 237.

genres.name: Hengchun narrative song
genres.note: Hengchun ballads on the southern peninsula use five moon-guitar tunes varied to fit Taiwanese tones. Chen Da (1905–1981) is the singer the 1999 Rough Guide calls legendary, and the same chapter says folk singers can still be heard there.

sources.citation: Wang Ying-fen, 'Taiwan: from innocence to funny rap', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides, 2000, book pp. 235–239.

genres.name: Kazakh akyn song
genres.note: Kazakh akyns are improvising bards. The 1999 Rough Guide centres Jambyl Jabayev, born in 1846, famous before the revolution, and still composing until his death at 99, so through 1945. His Soviet-era epics praised labour and Stalin while keeping the epic form.

sources.citation: Razia Sultanova and Simon Broughton, 'Central Asian Republics: bards of the golden road', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and Richard Trillo (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Latin and North America, Caribbean, India, Asia and Pacific, Rough Guides, 2000, book p. 24.

genres.name: Klasik
genres.note: Klasik is the Afghan name, taken from the English word classical, for the urban art music of Kabul. Kabuli ustads descend from musicians who came from India to play at the Afghan court in Kabul in the 1860s. The repertoire includes sung ghazals, instrumental naghmehs, and ragas. The rubab is its main instrument. The chapter's main centres are Kabul and Herat, drawn above a wider secondary practice in Kandahar and the southern Pashtun provinces, Balkh and the north, Badakhshan, the Hazarajat, the Panjshir valley as Parwan and Kapisa, and Logar, Nangarhar, and the east. The span runs from that court generation through the 1990s.

divisions.name: Ghazal
divisions.note: Ghazal is a vocal poetic form inside both Klasik and Afghan popular music. The Kabuli ghazal draws on Hindustani, Persian, and Pashtun practice. It is not a separate genre and has no record page; ghazal albums stay on the parent genre.

sources.citation: Veronica Doubleday, 'Afghanistan: red light at the crossroads', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and others (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Rough Guides, 2000, book pp. 3–7.

genres.name: Afghan popular music
genres.note: Afghan popular music was created at the Kabul radio station in the 1950s, when broadcasting began and a radio orchestra mixed Afghan lutes with harmonium, tabla, and European instruments. Parwin, Ahmad Zahir, and Mahwash shaped the verse-and-chorus radio style, which continued among Afghans in exile into the 2020s. Ghazal singing is part of this practice as well as of Klasik. The chapter names the dutar and the ghichak among its instruments.

genres.name: Afghan wedding and folk music
genres.note:
In Afghanistan, gender ideology profoundly affects musical life, as nearly all musical activity is segregated between women and men. Women perform primarily in small groups in domestic contexts, especially at private gatherings, weddings, and other rites of passage. The city of Herat was known for its professional female musicians, who had no parallels elsewhere in the country. 

These 1970s recordings of women and children singing love songs, lullabies, and melodies based on traditional quatrains (chahârbeit), accompanying themselves on large frame drums (dâireh), tabla, and Indian portable harmonium, capture a time before the civil wars and ongoing political unrest that severely disrupted Afghani music-making.

sources.citation: Veronica Doubleday, 'Afghanistan: red light at the crossroads', in Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham, and others (eds.), World Music: The Rough Guide, Volume 2, Rough Guides, 2000, book pp. 3–7.

genres.name: Contemporary Afghan music
genres.note:
After the 2001 US military intervention in Afghanistan the country witnesses the re-emergence of women in public sphere and re-integrating them in society. Afghanistan's musical culture started to revive, television went back on the air, while Radio Afghanistan put together a band of musicians and started broadcasting to an audience that was eager to hear music (Doubleday, 2011).

Both state and private television struggled to balance their programmes in terms of linguistic, ethnic, religious, confessional and musical diversity. It could be stated that the golden age of Pashtun traditional singing had arrived. Popular genres emerged as well. As a result, ‘Kabul Dreams’, one of the first local rock bands, was created in 2008. Their music was largely pop rock, with influences ranging from britpop to new wave punk, with a few folk motives interwoven. All members of the group fled Afghanistan in the 1990s, but after the Taliban regime fell, they returned with the objective of becoming Afghanistan's first big rockers, which they achieved.

sources.citation: Music Atlas chapter notes, roughguidegenres.md, Afghanistan, Contemporary Afghan Music, reviewed 2026-10-02.
